subject: Biology
text: Name the type of reproduction in Hydra.
modelAnswer: Hydra reproduces by budding — a type of asexual reproduction where a small outgrowth (bud) develops on the parent body, grows, and eventually separates to form a new individual.

Bud grows and detaches from parent

subject: Biology
text: Define parthenogenesis.
modelAnswer: Parthenogenesis is the development of a new organism from an unfertilised egg (ovum) without fertilisation. Example: drone (male honey bee) develops parthenogenetically from unfertilised eggs.
keyPoints: Development from unfertilised egg
Example: drones in honey bee

subject: Biology
text: What is implantation?
modelAnswer: Implantation is the process by which the blastocyst (early embryo) embeds itself into the endometrium (inner lining) of the uterus, approximately 7 days after fertilisation.
keyPoints: Blastocyst embeds in uterine endometrium
~7 days after fertilisation

subject: Biology
text: What is the full form of MTP? What is its significance?
modelAnswer: MTP: Medical Termination of Pregnancy. It is the deliberate ending of a pregnancy by medical procedures. It is significant for reproductive health as it helps avoid unwanted pregnancies and is legalised under strict conditions in India (MTP Act, 1971).

Deliberate ending of pregnancy
Legalised in India under MTP Act

subject: Biology
text: What are homologous chromosomes?
modelAnswer: Homologous chromosomes are pairs of chromosomes that carry genes for the same traits at corresponding loci (positions). One chromosome of each pair is inherited from each parent. They pair during meiosis (synapsis).
keyPoints: Pairs of chromosomes with same gene loci
One from each parent
Pair during meiosis

subject: Biology
text: Define co-dominance with an example.
modelAnswer: Co-dominance: both alleles in a heterozygote are fully expressed simultaneously in the phenotype. Example: blood group AB in humans — both Iᴬ and I᷾ alleles are expressed, producing both A and B antigens on red blood cells.
keyPoints: Both alleles expressed simultaneously
Example: blood group AB (Iᴬ I᷾)

subject: Biology
text: What are point mutations? Give an example.
modelAnswer: Point mutations are mutations involving a change in a single base pair of DNA. Example: sickle cell anaemia — a single nucleotide change (A→T) in the β-globin gene causes valine to replace glutamic acid at position 6.
keyPoints: Change in single base pair
Example: sickle cell anaemia (GAG→GTG)

subject: Biology
text: Name the enzyme that joins Okazaki fragments.
modelAnswer: DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand during DNA replication, linking the 3'-OH of one fragment to the 5'-phosphate of the next.
keyPoints: DNA ligase
Joins Okazaki fragments on lagging strand

subject: Biology
text: Define the term 'niche'.
modelAnswer: A niche is the functional role and position of an organism in its ecosystem — including all the resources it uses, the conditions it can tolerate, and its interactions with other species. No two species can occupy exactly the same niche (competitive exclusion principle).
keyPoints: Functional role in ecosystem
Includes resources, conditions, interactions
No two species share identical niche

subject: Biology
text: Give the reason: Why are offspring produced by sexual reproduction more variable than those produced by asexual reproduction?
modelAnswer: Sexual reproduction involves fusion of gametes from two parents, contributing genetic material from both. Meiosis and random fertilisation create new combinations of alleles. Asexual reproduction is mitotic — offspring are genetically identical to the parent (clones). Hence sexual reproduction produces more variation.
keyPoints: Sexual reproduction: meiosis + fusion of two parents' gametes
New allele combinations at each generation
Asexual: mitosis → clones, no variation

subject: Biology
text: Give the reason: Why do plants in a dense forest grow taller?
modelAnswer: In a dense forest, there is intense competition for sunlight (light is the limiting factor). Plants grow taller to reach sunlight above other competing plants. This is called etiolation or phototropic competition.
keyPoints: Competition for light (limiting resource)
Plants grow tall to overtop competitors
Light: major limiting factor in dense forests

subject: Biology
text: In ABO blood groups, what are the possible genotypes of a person with blood group O? If a group O man marries a group AB woman, what will be the blood groups of their children?
modelAnswer:
Blood group O: genotype I^i I^i (homozygous recessive).
Blood group AB: genotype I^A I^B.
Cross: I^i I^i × I^A I^B → offspring: I^A I^i (blood group A) and I^B I^i (blood group B) in 1:1 ratio.
Children will be 50% blood group A and 50% blood group B (no O or AB children).
keyPoints: O = i^i genotype
AB = I^A I^B
Offspring: 50% A (I^A i) and 50% B (I^B i)

subject: Biology
text: A colour-blind woman marries a normal man. What will be the phenotype of their sons and daughters regarding colour blindness?
modelAnswer:
Colour blindness (X-linked recessive). Colour-blind woman: X^c X^c. Normal man: X^N Y.
All sons: X^c Y (colour blind). All daughters: X^N X^c (carriers, normal vision).
So all sons are colour blind and all daughters are carriers (phenotypically normal).
keyPoints: Colour-blind woman: X^c X^c
All sons (X^c Y): colour blind
All daughters (X^N X^c): carrier, normal vision

subject: Biology
text: Mention the approximate life span and distinctive features of: (a) Ramapithecus; (b) Cro-Magnon man.
modelAnswer:
(a) Ramapithecus: lived ~14–7 million years ago. Small ape-like creature; walked semi-erect; had smaller canines and broader jaws than other apes; considered early human ancestor.
(b) Cro-Magnon man: Homo sapiens sapiens, lived ~30,000–10,000 years ago. Cave dweller; made tools, art, and paintings; used fire; modern humans; brain capacity ~1650 cc.

Cro-Magnon: 30,000-10,000 ya, modern H.sapiens, cave paintings, tools

subject: Biology
text: (a) Explain how global warming affects sea levels. (b) Name two methods to control noise pollution.
modelAnswer:
(a) Global warming melts polar ice caps and glaciers, adding water to oceans. Thermal expansion of seawater also occurs. Both effects raise sea levels, threatening coastal areas with flooding.
(b) Methods to control noise pollution: (i) Planting trees (green belts) along roads act as sound barriers; (ii) using ear muffs/plugs in industrial areas; (iii) making vehicles/machinery noise-efficient.
keyPoints: Global warming → ice melt + thermal expansion → sea level rise
Noise control: green belts, ear protection, noise-efficient machines

subject: Biology
text: What is BOD (Biological Oxygen Demand)? How does high BOD indicate water pollution?
modelAnswer:
BOD is the amount of oxygen (in ppm or mg/L) consumed by biological organisms when decomposing organic matter in a given water sample over a set period (5 days at 20°C).
High BOD indicates high organic matter in water — microbes decomposing it consume dissolved oxygen, leaving very little for aquatic life, causing fish kills and deterioration of water quality.
keyPoints: BOD: O₂ consumed to decompose organic matter (5 days, 20°C)
High BOD → high organic pollution
Low dissolved O₂ → kills aquatic life

subject: Biology
text: Distinguish between: (a) active and passive immunity; (b) benign and malignant tumour.
modelAnswer:
(a) Active immunity: body produces its own antibodies on exposure to antigen (e.g., vaccination). Long-lasting. Passive immunity: readymade antibodies given externally (e.g., anti-tetanus serum). Temporary.
(b) Benign tumour: enclosed in connective tissue, does not spread to other parts, localised and non-invasive. Malignant tumour (cancer): grows invasively, can metastasise (spread to other organs via blood/lymph).
keyPoints: Active: own antibodies; Passive: external antibodies
Benign: localised, non-spreading; Malignant: invasive, metastasises

subject: Biology
text: Mention two causes of male infertility.
modelAnswer: Causes of male infertility: (1) Low sperm count (oligospermia) or absence of sperm (azoospermia) due to hormonal imbalance, infections, or genetic factors. (2) Erectile dysfunction or poor sperm motility (asthenospermia). (3) Obstruction of vas deferens. (4) Chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., Klinefelter syndrome — XXY).
keyPoints: Low/absent sperm count (oligo/azoospermia)
Poor sperm motility, obstruction, or chromosomal abnormality

subject: Biology
text: What is gene therapy? Explain the treatment of SCID (Severe Combined Immunodeficiency) using gene therapy.
modelAnswer:
Gene therapy is the introduction of a functional copy of a defective gene into a patient's cells to correct a genetic disorder.
SCID treatment: SCID is caused by deficiency of adenosine deaminase (ADA) enzyme (due to mutation in ADA gene). Treatment steps: (1) Lymphocytes isolated from patient's blood. (2) Functional ADA gene introduced into lymphocytes using a retroviral vector ex vivo. (3) Engineered lymphocytes reinfused into patient. The cells now express ADA enzyme and restore immune function. (This requires periodic reinfusion as lymphocytes are mortal.)
keyPoints: Introduce functional gene to correct defect
SCID: ADA enzyme deficiency
ADA gene inserted via retroviral vector into patient's lymphocytes → reimplanted

subject: Biology
text: Explain industrial melanism in Biston betularia (peppered moth) as evidence for natural selection.
modelAnswer:
Biston betularia exists in two forms: pale speckled (typical) and dark melanic (carbonaria). Before industrialisation, pale form was common (camouflaged on lichen-covered tree bark); dark form was rare and easily eaten by birds.
During industrialisation, soot killed lichens and darkened tree trunks. Now dark moths were camouflaged; pale moths were conspicuous and preferentially eaten. Dark moths increased in industrial areas (natural selection favoured darker moths).
After pollution control, pale form recovered. This demonstrated that environmental changes can shift allele frequencies through natural selection.
keyPoints: Pre-industrial: pale form camouflaged on lichen bark
Post-industrial: dark bark → dark form survives
Demonstrates natural selection in action

subject: Biology
text: What is tissue culture? Explain any two applications of plant tissue culture.
modelAnswer:
Plant tissue culture: growing plant cells, tissues, or organs in vitro on nutrient medium under aseptic conditions. Based on totipotency — each plant cell can develop into a complete plant.
Applications: (1) Micropropagation: rapid clonal multiplication of plants (e.g., orchids, potatoes). (2) Production of virus-free plants: meristem culture free of viruses. (3) Somatic hybridization: protoplast fusion creates hybrid plants. (4) Production of somaclonal variants for crop improvement.
keyPoints: In vitro growth of plant cells/tissues on nutrient medium
Micropropagation: rapid multiplication
Virus-free plants via meristem culture

subject: Biology
text: Briefly explain: (a) spermiogenesis; (b) reproductive health; (c) amenorrhea.
modelAnswer:
(a) Spermiogenesis: transformation of spermatids (haploid) into functional spermatozoa. Involves condensation of nucleus, development of acrosome (from Golgi body), formation of tail (flagellum from centriole), shedding of excess cytoplasm.
(b) Reproductive health: total well-being in all aspects of reproduction — physical, emotional, social. Includes family planning, prevention of STDs, maternal health.
(c) Amenorrhea: absence or cessation of menstruation. Primary: failure to start menstruation by age 16. Secondary: cessation for 3+ months in women who previously menstruated (causes: pregnancy, menopause, stress, hormonal imbalance).
keyPoints: Spermiogenesis: spermatid→sperm (nucleus condensation, acrosome, tail formation)
Reproductive health: well-being in reproduction
Amenorrhea: absence of menstruation

subject: Biology
text: Briefly explain: (a) biodiversity hotspot; (b) Ramsar convention; (c) Red data book.
modelAnswer:
(a) Biodiversity hotspot: a region with exceptionally high species richness and endemism that has lost >70% of its original habitat. India has 4 hotspots: Himalayas, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Sundaland.
(b) Ramsar Convention (1971): international treaty for the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands. Wetlands listed as 'Ramsar sites' receive international protection.
(c) Red Data Book: a publication maintained by IUCN that lists threatened species of plants and animals, classified as Extinct, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, etc.
keyPoints: Hotspot: high endemism + >70% habitat loss
Ramsar: international wetland conservation treaty
Red Data Book: IUCN threatened species list

subject: Biology
text: Explain: (a) biodiversity loss due to habitat destruction; (b) eutrophication; (c) photosynthetically active radiation (PAR).
modelAnswer:
(a) Habitat destruction is the leading cause of biodiversity loss. Forest clearing, wetland drainage, and urbanisation eliminate the habitats that species need to survive, directly causing local extinctions.
(b) Eutrophication: excessive nutrients (N, P) from agricultural runoff or sewage enter water bodies → algal blooms → algae die → bacterial decomposition consumes O₂ → hypoxia kills fish (cultural eutrophication). Natural process is slow.
(c) PAR (Photosynthetically Active Radiation): solar radiation in the 400–700 nm wavelength range used by plants for photosynthesis. Plants absorb ~2-10% of total solar radiation as PAR for carbon fixation.
keyPoints: Habitat destruction: #1 cause of biodiversity loss
Eutrophication: excess nutrients → algal bloom → O₂ depletion
PAR: 400-700nm, used in photosynthesis

subject: Biology
text: Explain post-transcriptional modifications in eukaryotic mRNA. Why are these necessary?
modelAnswer:
Eukaryotic mRNA undergoes three main post-transcriptional modifications:
1. 5' capping: A 7-methylguanosine cap is added to the 5' end. Protects mRNA from degradation by exonucleases; helps in ribosome binding (translation initiation).
2. 3' polyadenylation: Poly-A tail (200-300 adenine nucleotides) added to 3' end. Protects from degradation; helps in export from nucleus; required for translation.
3. Splicing: Introns (non-coding sequences) are removed and exons (coding sequences) are joined by spliceosomes. This produces mature mRNA ready for translation. Differential splicing can produce multiple proteins from one gene.
These modifications are necessary to: protect mRNA from enzymatic degradation, aid export from nucleus, and ensure only coding sequences are translated.
keyPoints: 5' cap: protects from degradation, ribosome binding
3' poly-A tail: stability, export
Splicing: remove introns, join exons (mature mRNA)

subject: Biology
text: Describe the Avery, MacLeod and McCarty experiment (1944) that proved DNA is the genetic material.
modelAnswer:
Avery, MacLeod and McCarty extended Griffith's transformation experiment. They used S-strain (smooth, virulent) and R-strain (rough, non-virulent) Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Experiment: Cell-free extract of S-strain was treated with different enzymes and added to R-strain:
- Protease (destroys proteins): Transformation still occurred → protein not responsible.
- RNase (destroys RNA): Transformation still occurred → RNA not responsible.
- DNase (destroys DNA): Transformation did NOT occur → DNA is the transforming principle.
Conclusion: DNA is the genetic material responsible for transformation. This was the first direct biochemical proof that DNA carries genetic information.
keyPoints: DNase destroyed transformation; protease/RNase did not
DNA is the transforming principle (genetic material)
R-strain transformed to S-strain only when DNA present

subject: Biology
text: Explain the Chipko Movement. What were its objectives and outcomes?
modelAnswer:
Chipko Movement: a grassroots environmental movement in the Garhwal Himalayas, Uttarakhand, India, in 1973.
Origin: When contractors came to cut trees in Chamoli district, local women (led by Gaura Devi and inspired by Sunderlal Bahuguna) hugged ('chipko' = to cling/hug) the trees to prevent felling.
Objectives: (1) Protect forests from commercial exploitation. (2) Preserve forest-based livelihoods of local communities. (3) Prevent soil erosion and maintain water sources.
Outcomes: (1) Influenced the Indian government to ban commercial logging in the Himalayan forests in 1980. (2) Became a model for community-based conservation movements worldwide. (3) Highlighted the role of women in environmental protection.
keyPoints: 1973 Garhwal Himalayas; women hugged trees to prevent felling
Led by Gaura Devi; championed by Sunderlal Bahuguna
Led to logging ban in Himalayan forests 1980

subject: Biology
text: What is Joint Forest Management (JFM)? What are its features and significance?
modelAnswer:
Joint Forest Management (JFM): a programme of the Government of India (initiated 1988-90) that involves local communities (forest protection committees/village-level institutions) in the management and protection of forest land in partnership with state forest departments.
Features: (1) Local communities given rights to collect non-timber forest products (NTFPs). (2) Share of timber revenue given to communities. (3) Communities protect forests from illegal felling, fire, and encroachment.
Significance: (1) Reduces deforestation by involving local stakeholders with vested interest. (2) Improves livelihood of forest-dependent communities. (3) Promotes biodiversity conservation. (4) Forests regenerate as communities prevent overuse.
keyPoints: Community-forest department partnership in forest management
Communities get NTFPs and revenue share in exchange for protection
Initiated 1988; reduces deforestation, improves livelihoods

subject: Biology
text: Describe the steps of PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction). Why is Taq polymerase used?
modelAnswer:
PCR amplifies specific DNA sequences in vitro through repeated thermal cycles:
1. Denaturation (94°C): Heat separates double-stranded DNA into single strands.
2. Annealing (50-65°C): Specific short DNA primers (oligonucleotides) bind to complementary sequences flanking the target region.
3. Extension (72°C): Taq DNA polymerase extends the primers, synthesising new DNA strands using the template.
This cycle (denaturation → annealing → extension) is repeated 30-40 times, doubling DNA each cycle → 2ⁿ copies.
Taq polymerase: isolated from Thermus aquaticus (hot spring bacterium). It is thermostable — remains active at 94°C denaturation temperature unlike regular DNA polymerases that would denature.
keyPoints: 3 steps: denaturation (94°C), annealing, extension (72°C)
Taq polymerase: thermostable (from Thermus aquaticus)
~2ⁿ copies after n cycles

subject: Biology
text: Explain the Blue-White selection method used to identify recombinant clones.
modelAnswer:
Blue-White selection is used to identify bacterial colonies containing a recombinant plasmid (with insert) vs. non-recombinant (no insert).
Method: The cloning vector contains the lacZ gene (encoding β-galactosidase). When a foreign DNA fragment is inserted into the Multiple Cloning Site (MCS) within lacZ, the lacZ gene is disrupted.
When bacteria are grown on medium containing X-gal (a chromogenic substrate) and IPTG:
- Non-recombinant colonies (intact lacZ): β-galactosidase cleaves X-gal → blue colour.
- Recombinant colonies (disrupted lacZ): no active β-galactosidase → white colour.
White colonies are picked for further analysis — they contain the recombinant plasmid with insert.
keyPoints: Insert disrupts lacZ gene in MCS
X-gal medium: non-recombinant = blue (active lacZ)
Recombinant = white (disrupted lacZ)
Select white colonies for recombinants

subject: Biology
text: In an enzyme experiment, a student preheated enzyme D-42 (amylase) at 90°C for 10 minutes before adding it to starch solution. What was the purpose of this preheating step?
modelAnswer: Preheating amylase at 90°C denatures the enzyme — the high temperature disrupts its tertiary structure (hydrogen bonds, disulfide bridges) and destroys its active site. This serves as a control to demonstrate that it is the active (native) enzyme that causes starch digestion, not some other component. The preheated (denatured) enzyme should show no starch hydrolysis.
keyPoints: 90°C denatures the enzyme (destroys active site)
Control to confirm enzyme is responsible for digestion
Denatured enzyme shows no activity

subject: Biology
text: What is the end product of starch digestion by amylase (enzyme D-42)?
modelAnswer: The end product of starch digestion by amylase is maltose (disaccharide). Salivary and pancreatic amylase both cleave the α-1,4-glycosidic bonds of starch, converting starch → dextrins → maltose. Maltose is then further hydrolysed by maltase to glucose.
keyPoints: Amylase hydrolyses α-1,4-glycosidic bonds
End product: maltose (disaccharide)
Further hydrolysed to glucose by maltase

subject: Biology
text: In an enzyme experiment with amylase and starch, one tube (with active enzyme) showed negative iodine test while another (with boiled enzyme) showed positive iodine test. What conclusions can you draw?
modelAnswer:
Conclusion 1: Active amylase digested starch → negative iodine test (iodine gives blue-black only with starch). This confirms amylase's enzymatic activity.
Conclusion 2: Denatured (boiled) enzyme failed to digest starch → positive iodine test (starch remains). This shows that protein's three-dimensional structure (active site) is essential for enzymatic activity.
Overall conclusion: Enzymes are proteins; denaturation inactivates them; the active site must be intact for catalysis.
keyPoints: Active enzyme: starch digested → iodine negative
Boiled enzyme: starch intact → iodine positive
Conclusion: intact protein structure required for enzyme activity

subject: Biology
text: Give one significant contribution of each of the following scientists: (i) Wallace (ii) R. Mishra (iii) G. Gamow (iv) Sanger
modelAnswer:

subject: Biology
text: Define: (i) Carrying capacity (ii) Homologous chromosomes
modelAnswer:
(i) Carrying capacity (K): The maximum population size of a species that an environment can sustain indefinitely, given the food, habitat, water, and other resources available. When population reaches K, growth rate becomes zero.
(ii) Homologous chromosomes: A pair of chromosomes (one from each parent) that are similar in size, shape, gene loci order, and centromere position. They pair during meiosis. One is maternal and one is paternal in origin.

homologous chromosomes: similar size/shape, pair in meiosis

subject: Biology
text: Give a reason for each of: (i) Bagging is essential in artificial hybridisation. (ii) Climax stage is achieved quickly in secondary succession compared to primary succession.
modelAnswer:
(i) Bagging is essential to prevent contamination of the stigma by unwanted pollen. The emasculated flower is covered with a bag (usually polythene or butter paper) to prevent foreign pollen from reaching the stigma before desired cross-pollination is performed.
(ii) In secondary succession, the soil is already present with nutrients and often contains dormant seeds and vegetative propagules, so plants can establish quickly. In primary succession, soil formation itself must occur first from bare rock, which is a very slow process. Hence climax is reached faster in secondary succession.
keyPoints: bagging: prevent contamination by unwanted pollen
secondary succession: soil + dormant seeds present → faster
primary succession: soil must form first from bare rock

subject: Biology
text: Enumerate any four essential features of good and effective poultry farm management practices.
modelAnswer:

subject: Biology
text: What is reproductive fitness? Explain it with the help of an example.
modelAnswer:
Reproductive fitness (Darwinian fitness): The ability of an organism to survive and reproduce in its environment, resulting in greater contribution of offspring to the next generation. It is a measure of how successfully an organism passes its genes to the next generation.

Secondary lymphoid organs: Sites where lymphocytes interact with antigens and initiate immune responses. They trap antigens from the body. Examples: spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue).

subject: Biology
text: Explain the evolution of long neck of giraffe according to Charles Darwin.
modelAnswer:
According to Darwin's theory of Natural Selection:
1. In the ancestral giraffe population, there was natural variation — some individuals had slightly longer necks than others.
2. There was competition for food (leaves from tall trees); giraffes with longer necks could reach higher branches.
3. Natural selection: Giraffes with longer necks had better survival advantage — they could access more food, especially during scarcity. These individuals survived and reproduced (survival of the fittest).
4. Inheritance: The longer neck trait was inherited by offspring.
5. Over many generations, the proportion of long-necked individuals increased.
6. Gradually, through accumulated changes over thousands of generations, the population evolved to have long necks.
(Note: Darwin's explanation is in contrast to Lamarck's 'use and disuse' theory. Darwin emphasised selection of pre-existing variation, not use-induced changes.)

longer neck = advantage in reaching food (survival of fittest)
inherited trait → frequency increases over generations

text: Describe the structure of a nucleosome with the help of a well-labelled diagram.
modelAnswer:
Nucleosome: The basic repeating unit of chromatin.
Structure:

subject: Biology
text: (a) Explain the Rivet Popper hypothesis.
modelAnswer:
The Rivet Popper hypothesis was proposed by Paul Ehrlich. He used the analogy of an aeroplane to explain the importance of biodiversity:
- An aeroplane (ecosystem) is held together by many rivets (species). Each rivet contributes to the structural integrity of the plane.
- Removing a few rivets (losing a few species) may not immediately affect the plane's function, but weakens it.
- As more rivets (species) are removed, the plane (ecosystem) becomes increasingly unstable.
- Eventually, the loss of too many rivets causes catastrophic failure (ecosystem collapse).
- This illustrates that even apparently 'useless' species may be crucial for ecosystem function, and loss of biodiversity weakens ecosystems.
keyPoints: aeroplane = ecosystem; rivets = species
removing rivets weakens structure gradually
too many losses → catastrophic ecosystem collapse

subject: Biology
text: (b) Define: (1) Standing crop, (2) Stenothermal organisms, (3) Niche.
modelAnswer:
(1) Standing crop: The total amount of living organic material (biomass) present in a particular area or trophic level of an ecosystem at a given time. It includes both above-ground and below-ground biomass.
(2) Stenothermal organisms: Organisms that can tolerate only a narrow range of temperature. They are sensitive to temperature fluctuations. Examples: snow leopard, polar bear (cold-adapted), some corals (warm-adapted).
(3) Niche (ecological niche): The functional role and position of an organism in its ecosystem — the total set of biotic and abiotic conditions in which an organism lives and the way it uses resources. No two species can occupy the same niche simultaneously in the same habitat (competitive exclusion principle).
keyPoints: standing crop: biomass at a given time in an area
stenothermal: narrow temperature tolerance
niche: functional role + resource use in ecosystem

subject: Biology
text: Explain the different types of endosperms in angiosperms.
modelAnswer:
Endosperm is the nutritive tissue formed after fertilisation (triple fusion — 2 polar nuclei + sperm nucleus → triploid endosperm nucleus). Types:
1. Nuclear endosperm: Primary endosperm nucleus divides repeatedly without wall formation first; many free nuclei formed, later walls develop. Most common type (e.g., coconut milk is free nuclear endosperm; coconut flesh is cellular endosperm).
2. Cellular endosperm: Each division of the endosperm nucleus is accompanied by wall formation, so cells form from the beginning. Example: Datura, Adoxa.
3. Helobial endosperm: First division forms two chambers (micropylar and chalazal); nuclear type in one chamber and cellular in the other. Intermediate type. Found in monocots.
keyPoints: nuclear: free nuclei first, walls later (coconut)

subject: Biology
text: (a) Describe the physico-chemical events that take place during fertilization in humans.
modelAnswer:
Fertilisation in humans occurs in the ampullary-isthmic junction of the fallopian tube:
1. Capacitation: Sperms undergo changes in the female reproductive tract (increased motility, membrane changes).
2. Acrosomal reaction: On contact with zona pellucida of the secondary oocyte, the acrosome of the sperm releases hydrolytic enzymes (hyaluronidase, acrosin).
3. Penetration of zona pellucida: Enzymes + motility of sperm help it penetrate the zona pellucida.
4. Plasma membrane fusion: Sperm membrane fuses with the oocyte membrane. Entry of sperm nucleus triggers oocyte to complete meiosis II (oocyte was arrested at metaphase II).
5. Cortical reaction (block to polyspermy): Cortical granules release enzymes that harden the zona pellucida, preventing entry of other sperms.
6. Amphimixis: Male and female pronuclei form and fuse, restoring the diploid number (2n = 46). Zygote is formed.
keyPoints: acrosomal reaction: hyaluronidase released
penetration of zona pellucida
cortical reaction: prevents polyspermy; pronuclei fuse → zygote (2n)

subject: Biology
text: (b) Answer: (i) Define and give the role of amniocentesis. (ii) Causative agent and one symptom of Gonorrhoea. (iii) Significance of dispersal of seeds (two points). (iv) What are seasonal breeders? Give an example. (v) How is chromosome number maintained in sexually reproducing organisms?
modelAnswer:
(i) Amniocentesis: A foetal sex determination technique involving withdrawal of a small amount of amniotic fluid from the amniotic sac. The foetal cells are cultured and chromosomes examined. Role: Detecting chromosomal abnormalities (Down syndrome, trisomy), sex determination (though banned in India for sex determination). Used to detect genetic disorders.
(ii) Gonorrhoea: Caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae (bacterium). Symptom: Burning sensation and pain during urination; discharge of pus from urethra/vagina.
(iii) Significance of seed dispersal: (1) Prevents overcrowding and competition between parent and offspring plants for light, nutrients, and space. (2) Colonisation of new habitats, increasing species range and distribution.
(iv) Seasonal breeders: Animals that breed only at specific times of the year, usually responding to environmental cues like photoperiod (day length) or temperature. Example: frogs (breed in monsoon), deer.
(v) Chromosome number is maintained through meiosis during gametogenesis. Each gamete (egg and sperm) has haploid number (n) of chromosomes. When two gametes fuse during fertilisation, the diploid number (2n) is restored. This ensures chromosome number remains constant from generation to generation.
keyPoints: amniocentesis: amniotic fluid analysis for chromosomal abnormalities
Gonorrhoea: Neisseria gonorrhoeae; burning urination, pus discharge
seed dispersal: prevents competition, colonises new habitats; meiosis maintains chromosome number

subject: Biology
text: (a)(i) What are restriction endonucleases? Give the rules of their nomenclature. (ii) Explain the mechanism of action that makes them suitable for genetic engineering.
modelAnswer:
(i) Restriction endonucleases (restriction enzymes): Molecular scissors — enzymes that cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences (recognition sites), producing defined fragments. They are produced by bacteria as a defence against foreign DNA (bacteriophages).
Nomenclature rules:
- First letter: genus of the bacterium (italicised, capitalised)
- Next two letters: species of the bacterium
- Fourth letter: strain (if any)
- Roman numeral: order of discovery in that organism
Example: EcoRI — Escherichia (E) coli (co) strain R (R), first enzyme (I).
(ii) Mechanism: Restriction enzymes recognise specific palindromic sequences (read same on both strands in 5'→3' direction). They cut both strands of the double helix, either producing: (a) Sticky ends (cohesive ends): staggered cuts leaving short single-stranded overhangs — preferred for cloning as complementary ends can hybridise with other fragments. (b) Blunt ends: even cuts leaving no overhangs. The specific cutting sites and sticky ends allow insertion of desired DNA into vectors for genetic engineering.
keyPoints: restriction enzymes: cut DNA at palindromic sequences
nomenclature: genus-species-strain-order (e.g., EcoRI)
sticky ends: preferred for cloning; cut at palindromic sites

subject: Biology
text: (b)(i) Explain desirable characteristics of an ideal cloning vector used in rDNA technology. (ii) Describe two vectorless methods of gene transfer.
modelAnswer:
(i) Desirable characteristics of an ideal cloning vector:
1. Origin of replication (ori): To replicate independently in the host cell.
2. Selectable marker: Gene for antibiotic resistance (e.g., ampR, tetR) to identify transformed cells.
3. Cloning sites: Multiple restriction sites (MCS) for insertion of foreign DNA.
4. Low copy number or high copy number depending on application.
5. Small size: Easy to handle and transform.
6. Compatible with host: Able to replicate in the intended host organism.
7. Should be non-pathogenic and safe.
(ii) Vectorless methods of gene transfer:
1. Biolistics (gene gun): DNA is coated onto gold or tungsten microparticles (micro-projectiles) and bombarded at high speed into plant cells/tissues using a gene gun. DNA enters cells and integrates into the genome.
2. Microinjection: Foreign DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an animal cell using a fine glass micropipette (microneedle). Used in animals, embryos.
Others: Electroporation (electric pulse to make pores in cell membrane), chemical method (calcium phosphate, polyethylene glycol).
keyPoints: cloning vector: ori, selectable marker, restriction sites, small size
biolistics: DNA-coated gold particles shot into cells (gene gun)
microinjection: DNA directly injected into nucleus

subject: Biology
text: (a) Give a graphic representation of the carbon cycle in nature.
modelAnswer:
Carbon cycle diagram showing:
1. Atmospheric CO₂ pool
2. Photosynthesis: Plants (and algae) fix atmospheric CO₂ → organic carbon (glucose, etc.)
3. Respiration: All organisms (plants, animals, microbes) release CO₂ back to atmosphere
4. Feeding: Animals consume plants → carbon passes through food chain
5. Decomposition: Decomposers break down dead matter → CO₂ released
6. Combustion: Burning of fossil fuels (coal, oil), forest fires → CO₂ to atmosphere
7. Ocean exchange: CO₂ dissolves in oceans ↔ atmosphere
8. Sedimentation: Some carbon buried as fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, natural gas)
The cycle shows interconversion between atmospheric, biotic, and abiotic carbon reservoirs.

subject: Biology
text: (b) Give a graphic representation of the phosphorus cycle in nature.
modelAnswer:
Phosphorus cycle (sedimentary cycle — no atmospheric component):
1. Weathering of rocks: Phosphate minerals (apatite) dissolved by water → phosphates enter soil
2. Plants absorb inorganic phosphate (PO₄³⁻) from soil → organic phosphorus in plant tissues
3. Consumers: Animals eat plants → phosphorus passes through food chain
4. Decomposition: Decomposers break down dead organisms → phosphorus returned to soil as inorganic phosphate
5. Runoff: Phosphates washed into rivers/oceans → taken up by aquatic organisms
6. Sedimentation: Phosphate deposits on ocean floor → geological uplift → weathering releases again
7. Leaching: Excess phosphate may leach into groundwater
Note: Phosphorus cycle is a sedimentary (non-gaseous) biogeochemical cycle — no atmospheric phase.
keyPoints: weathering of rocks → phosphate in soil
plants absorb phosphate → food chain
decomposition → inorganic phosphate (sedimentary cycle, no atmospheric phase)

subject: Biology

subject: Biology
text: Give one significant difference between the following: (i) Linkage and crossing over (ii) Transition and transversion
modelAnswer:
(i) Linkage: Linkage is the tendency of genes located on the same chromosome to be inherited together without separation. Crossing over is the exchange of chromosomal segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during meiosis I, which breaks linkage groups and creates new combinations of alleles (recombinants).

(ii) Transition: A type of point mutation where a purine is replaced by another purine (A↔G) or a pyrimidine by another pyrimidine (C↔T). Transversion: A point mutation where a purine is replaced by a pyrimidine or vice versa (A or G ↔ C or T). Transversions cause greater structural change in the DNA.
keyPoints: Linkage: genes inherited together; Crossing over: exchange breaks linkage

Transversion: purine↔pyrimidine

text: Explain two characteristics of cancer cells.
modelAnswer:
1. Uncontrolled cell division (loss of cell cycle regulation): Cancer cells lose the normal regulatory mechanisms (tumour suppressor genes like p53 are inactivated; oncogenes are activated) and divide continuously and uncontrollably, forming a tumour/neoplasm.

2. Metastasis: Cancer cells have the ability to detach from the primary tumour, invade surrounding tissues, enter blood/lymph vessels, and migrate to distant organs where they establish new tumours (secondary tumours). This makes cancer difficult to treat.
keyPoints: Uncontrolled proliferation: loss of cell cycle control
Metastasis: spread to other organs through blood/lymph
Contact inhibition lost in cancer cells

modelAnswer:
(a) Germinating pollen grain labels: Pollen wall (exine and intine), Generative cell (or male gametes), Tube nucleus (vegetative nucleus), Pollen tube, Tip of pollen tube (where gametes are released), Germination pore (aperture/colpus)

(b) Mature human ovum labels: Zona pellucida (outer protective glycoprotein coat), Corona radiata (outer layer of follicular cells), Cell membrane (plasma membrane/oolemma), Nucleus (in secondary oocyte stage, at second meiotic metaphase), Cytoplasm (with yolk), First polar body (between zona pellucida and plasma membrane)

Ovum: zona pellucida, corona radiata, nucleus, first polar body

subject: Biology
text: What is outbreeding? How is it useful in animal breeding?
modelAnswer:
Outbreeding is the practice of mating animals that are unrelated and not sharing common ancestors for 4–6 generations. It is the opposite of inbreeding. Types include: outcrossing (mating within same breed but no common ancestry), crossbreeding (mating different breeds), and interspecific hybridization.

Usefulness: Overcomes inbreeding depression; increases heterozygosity; enhances fertility and productivity; improves immune system; helps in obtaining hybrid vigour (heterosis) for superior performance in milk yield, growth rate, resistance to disease.
keyPoints: Mating unrelated individuals from different breeds
Overcomes inbreeding depression
Enhances productivity through hybrid vigour/heterosis

subject: Biology
text: (a) What is biomagnification? Write two effects of biomagnification. OR (b) Write a short note on the contribution of Ahmed Khan of Bangalore.
modelAnswer:
(a) Biomagnification (bioaccumulation): The progressive increase in the concentration of non-biodegradable or slowly degradable toxins (like DDT, heavy metals) at successive trophic levels in a food chain. Each consumer accumulates higher concentrations than its prey.

Two effects:
1. Top predators (eagles, large fish, humans) accumulate the highest concentrations, causing reproductive failure, eggshell thinning in birds (DDT), organ damage, and death.
2. Bald eagles and osprey populations declined due to DDT accumulation causing thin eggshells; similar effects documented in humans causing cancer and hormonal disruption.

(b) Ahmed Khan of Bangalore is known for his pioneering work in waste management. He started 'Waste Wise' in Bangalore and advocated for waste segregation at source and waste-to-energy approaches. He demonstrated that municipal solid waste can be managed efficiently through community participation, composting organic waste, and recycling, significantly reducing landfill burden.
keyPoints: Biomagnification: toxin concentration increases up food chain
Effects: reproductive failure in top predators, DDT eggshell thinning
Ahmed Khan: waste management pioneer, Waste Wise, Bangalore

subject: Biology
text: Give three adaptations in organisms by which they avoid predation.
modelAnswer:
Three adaptations to avoid predation:

1. Cryptic colouration (Camouflage): Organisms have body colour that blends with their background, making them difficult for predators to detect. Example: praying mantis resembles a leaf; chameleons change colour.

2. Mimicry: Some prey species resemble other dangerous or distasteful species. Batesian mimicry: harmless species resembles a harmful/toxic one (e.g., non-venomous king snake mimics venomous coral snake). Müllerian mimicry: two toxic species resemble each other.

3. Chemical defence: Many organisms produce noxious chemicals, venoms, or toxic substances to deter predators. Examples: monarch butterfly caterpillars store toxins from milkweed; bombardier beetle sprays hot chemical spray; poison dart frogs secrete skin toxins.
keyPoints: Camouflage: blend with background (chameleon, stick insect)
Mimicry: Batesian and Müllerian
Chemical defence: toxic secretions (poison frogs, monarch butterfly)

subject: Biology
text: (a) Define decomposition. Explain main steps involved in the process of decomposition. OR (b) Write three causes and three effects of cultural eutrophication.
modelAnswer:
(a) Decomposition: The process by which decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down complex organic matter (dead organic matter/detritus) into simpler inorganic substances like CO₂, H₂O, and mineral salts.

Main steps:
1. Fragmentation: Detritivores (earthworms, millipedes) break detritus into smaller particles, increasing surface area.
2. Leaching: Water-soluble nutrients move down into lower soil layers (leaching into the soil).
3. Catabolism: Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler organic substances (humification precursor).
4. Humification: Dark, amorphous, colloidal organic material (humus) is formed. Humus is resistant to decomposition and enriches soil.
5. Mineralisation: Inorganic nutrients (N, P, K) are released from humus by further microbial action, making them available for plant uptake.

(b) Cultural eutrophication:
Causes: Discharge of agricultural run-off (fertilizers with N and P); discharge of sewage effluents; industrial effluents containing nutrients
Effects: Excessive algal bloom (algae proliferate on surface); depletion of dissolved oxygen (O₂) as decomposers break down dead algae; death of aquatic animals (fish kills) due to oxygen depletion
keyPoints: Decomposition: fragmentation → leaching → catabolism → humification → mineralisation
Eutrophication causes: fertilizer runoff, sewage, industrial effluents
Eutrophication effects: algal bloom, oxygen depletion, fish kills

subject: Biology
text: (i) Write two differences between homologous organs and analogous organs. (ii) Give one example of homologous organs and one example of analogous organs found in plants.
modelAnswer:
(i) Differences:
Homologous organs: Have the same basic structural plan (same embryonic origin) but perform different functions; result of divergent evolution. Example: forelimb of horse, bat wing, human arm.
Analogous organs: Have different structural origin/plan but perform similar functions; result of convergent evolution. Example: wings of birds and insects.

(ii) Plant examples:
Homologous organs in plants: Thorns of Bougainvillea and tendrils of Cucurbita (both are stem modifications, same origin)
Analogous organs in plants: Tendrils of pea (Pisum sativum — leaf modification) and tendrils of Cucurbita/cucumber (stem modification) — same function (support/climbing) but different origin
keyPoints: Homologous: same origin, different function (divergent evolution)
Analogous: different origin, same function (convergent evolution)
Homologous in plants: Bougainvillea thorn and Cucurbita tendril (both stem)

subject: Biology
text: Describe the process of double fertilization in angiosperms. What is its significance?
modelAnswer:
Double fertilization in angiosperms:
1. Pollen grain germinates on stigma, pollen tube grows through style to the ovule.
2. Pollen tube releases two male gametes (non-motile sperms) into the embryo sac.
3. First fertilization: One sperm fuses with the egg cell (n + n) → zygote (2n) → develops into embryo (syngamy/true fertilization)
4. Second fertilization: The other sperm fuses with the two polar nuclei (n + n + n) → primary endosperm nucleus (3n) → develops into endosperm (triple fusion/triple fertilization)

Significance:
1. Produces the embryo (ensures genetic continuity and variation through sexual reproduction)
2. Produces triploid (3n) endosperm which provides nutrition to the developing embryo — ensures efficient energy use (endosperm only develops when fertilization occurs, preventing wastage of resources)
keyPoints: Syngamy: sperm + egg → 2n zygote → embryo
Triple fusion: sperm + 2 polar nuclei → 3n endosperm
Significance: genetic continuity + nutritional efficiency

subject: Biology
text: What is a bioreactor? Explain important features of a Stirred tank bioreactor.
modelAnswer:
Bioreactor: A vessel/apparatus in which living organisms (bacteria, fungi, animal cells) or their enzymes are used to carry out biochemical reactions under optimally controlled conditions for production of useful substances (antibiotics, vaccines, enzymes, insulin).

Important features of Stirred tank bioreactor:
1. Agitator/stirrer: A rotating stirrer (impeller) that continuously mixes the contents to ensure uniform distribution of nutrients, oxygen, and heat throughout the culture medium.
2. Sparger: A device at the bottom that introduces sterile air/oxygen as fine bubbles for aeration of the culture.
3. Temperature control: A jacketed vessel with temperature sensors and heating/cooling coils maintains optimal temperature for microbial growth.
4. pH control: pH sensors and addition of acid/base to maintain optimal pH.
5. Foam control: Antifoam agents or mechanical foam breakers prevent excessive foaming.
6. Sampling port: For withdrawing samples without contamination.
keyPoints: Bioreactor: controlled vessel for biological reactions
Stirrer: uniform mixing
Sparger: aeration
Temperature and pH control
Foam control

subject: Biology
text: Give three significant differences between asexual reproduction and sexual reproduction.
modelAnswer:
Differences between asexual and sexual reproduction:

1. Gametes: Asexual reproduction does not involve gametes or fertilization; offspring arise from a single parent by mitosis. Sexual reproduction involves formation and fusion of gametes (male and female); involves meiosis and fertilization.

2. Genetic variation: Offspring in asexual reproduction are genetically identical to the parent (clones), hence no variation. In sexual reproduction, offspring show genetic variation due to meiosis (crossing over, independent assortment) and random fusion of gametes.

3. Speed and energy: Asexual reproduction is faster and requires less energy; more offspring produced rapidly. Sexual reproduction is slower and requires more energy but produces diverse offspring better adapted to changing environments.
keyPoints: Asexual: no gametes, single parent, mitosis, clones
Sexual: gametes, two parents, meiosis, variation
Asexual: faster; Sexual: genetically diverse

subject: Biology
text: (a) Explain the process of spermatogenesis in humans. OR (b) Give an account of hormonal control of oogenesis.
modelAnswer:
(a) Spermatogenesis in humans:
1. Spermatogonia (2n) in seminiferous tubules undergo mitosis to produce primary spermatocytes (2n).
2. Primary spermatocytes undergo meiosis I (reductive division) to produce two secondary spermatocytes (n).
3. Secondary spermatocytes undergo meiosis II to produce 4 spermatids (n).
4. Spermatids undergo spermiogenesis (differentiation): acrosome forms from Golgi, flagellum from centriole, nuclear condensation → spermatozoa.
5. Spermiation: spermatozoa released from Sertoli cells into seminiferous tubule lumen.
Regulation: FSH stimulates Sertoli cells; LH (ICSH) stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone which drives spermatogenesis.

(b) Hormonal control of oogenesis:
1. FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) from anterior pituitary stimulates growth of primary follicles.
2. Estrogen from growing follicle provides positive feedback on LH surge.
3. LH surge (around day 14) triggers ovulation — release of secondary oocyte.
4. Progesterone from corpus luteum (formed from ruptured follicle under LH) maintains endometrium if fertilization occurs.
5. If no fertilization, corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone/estrogen fall, menstruation occurs.
keyPoints: Spermatogonia → primary spermatocyte → secondary spermatocyte → spermatids → sperm
FSH, LH (ICSH), testosterone regulate spermatogenesis
Oogenesis: FSH → follicle, LH surge → ovulation, progesterone → corpus luteum

subject: Biology
text: (a) Explain the various steps involved in Recombinant DNA technology. OR (b) Explain the steps involved in the production of human insulin by Recombinant DNA technology.
modelAnswer:
(a) Steps in Recombinant DNA technology:
1. Isolation of DNA: Extract and purify the desired gene from the organism.
2. Cutting of DNA (Restriction digestion): Use restriction endonucleases (molecular scissors) to cut the desired gene and the vector DNA at specific recognition sequences, producing sticky ends.
3. Insertion into vector: Ligate the gene into the vector (plasmid, phage) using DNA ligase to form recombinant DNA.
4. Introduction into host: Transform/transfect the recombinant vector into host cells (bacteria, yeast) by electroporation, heat shock, microinjection.
5. Selection of recombinants: Identify host cells containing the desired gene (using antibiotic resistance markers, blue-white screening).
6. Cloning and expression: Grow selected cells to produce many copies; induce gene expression to produce the protein of interest.
7. Downstream processing: Isolate, purify, and formulate the protein product.

(b) Human insulin by rDNA technology (Eli Lilly method):
1. Human insulin gene (A-chain and B-chain) synthesized chemically (or obtained from pancreatic cDNA).
2. Inserted separately into E. coli plasmids using restriction enzymes and ligase.
3. Each plasmid also carries lac Z gene fused with insulin chain gene.
4. E. coli transformed, grown in fermenters.
5. Produces A-chain and B-chain fused with beta-galactosidase.
6. Chains extracted, treated with cyanogen bromide to separate insulin chains from beta-galactosidase.
7. A-chain and B-chain combined chemically with disulphide bonds → active human insulin (Humulin).
keyPoints: rDNA: isolation, restriction digestion, ligation, transformation, selection, expression
Human insulin: A and B chains produced separately in E. coli
Chains combined with disulfide bonds → Humulin

subject: Biology
text: (a)(i) Give an account of Meselson and Stahl's experiment. (ii) What is the significance of Meselson and Stahl's experiment? OR (b)(i) Describe the Oparin Haldane Theory of origin of life. (ii) The tadpole larva of amphibians resembles fishes. How does this observation support evolution?
modelAnswer:
(a)(i) Meselson and Stahl's experiment (1958) — proof of semi-conservative DNA replication:
1. E. coli grown in ¹⁵NH₄Cl (heavy nitrogen) for many generations → all DNA labeled with ¹⁵N (heavy DNA).
2. Transferred to ¹⁴N medium and grown for one generation → DNA isolated and centrifuged in CsCl density gradient.
3. Result: All DNA appeared as a single intermediate density band (hybrid ¹⁵N-¹⁴N DNA).
4. After second generation: Two bands — one intermediate (¹⁵N-¹⁴N) and one light (¹⁴N-¹⁴N) in equal ratio.
(ii) Significance: Confirmed that DNA replication is semi-conservative — each new DNA molecule contains one old (parental) strand and one newly synthesized strand. Ruled out conservative (both old strands together) and dispersive replication.

(b)(i) Oparin-Haldane theory (Primordial Soup / Chemical Evolution):
- Early Earth had a reducing atmosphere (CH₄, NH₃, H₂O, H₂, no O₂).
- Energy from lightning, UV radiation, and heat drove abiotic synthesis of simple organic molecules (amino acids, sugars) — Miller-Urey experiment confirmed this.
- These accumulated in the primitive ocean forming a 'primordial soup'.
- Spontaneous condensation formed complex molecules (proteins, nucleic acids).
- Aggregates (coacervates, microspheres) formed that could absorb nutrients and grow.
- Over millions of years, the first living cells evolved from these aggregates.

(ii) Tadpole larva of amphibians has fish-like characteristics (tail, gills, aquatic lifestyle) because ancestral amphibians evolved from fish ancestors. Ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny (Ernst Haeckel's biogenetic law): the developmental stages of an organism briefly reflect its evolutionary history, supporting descent with modification.
keyPoints: Meselson-Stahl: ¹⁵N to ¹⁴N medium; hybrid band after 1 gen; semi-conservative replication
Oparin-Haldane: reducing atmosphere, primordial soup, abiotic synthesis, coacervates
Tadpole resembles fish: biogenetic law, amphibians evolved from fish ancestors

subject: Biology
text: (a) Draw a labelled diagram to show the life cycle of Plasmodium. OR (b) Draw a labelled diagram to show replication of HIV in human cells.
modelAnswer:
(a) Life cycle of Plasmodium (malaria parasite):
In mosquito (sexual cycle/sporogony): 
- Anopheles mosquito ingests gametocytes from infected human blood
- Gametes form in mosquito stomach → fertilization → zygote → ookinete → oocyst → sporozoites
- Sporozoites migrate to salivary glands

In human host (asexual cycle):
- Pre-erythrocytic (liver) stage: sporozoites from mosquito bite enter liver cells (hepatocytes) → schizogony → merozoites released
- Erythrocytic stage: merozoites enter RBCs → ring stage → trophozoite → schizont → multiple merozoites released (cause fever at 48-72 hr intervals) → some form gametocytes

Labels: sporozoites, liver cells, merozoites, RBC, ring stage trophozoite, schizont, gametocytes, mosquito gut

(b) HIV replication in human cells (T-helper/CD4⁺ cells):
1. HIV binds to CD4 receptor and co-receptor (CCR5/CXCR4) on T-helper cell
2. Viral envelope fuses with cell membrane; viral core enters cytoplasm
3. Reverse transcriptase converts viral RNA → single-stranded DNA → double-stranded DNA (provirus)
4. Proviral DNA integrates into host chromosome (integrase enzyme)
5. Provirus transcribed by host RNA polymerase → viral RNA and mRNA
6. mRNA translated → viral proteins (protease cleaves polyprotein)
7. New viral particles assembled, bud off from cell membrane
8. Mature HIV released, infects more CD4⁺ cells; T-helper cell count declines → AIDS
keyPoints: Plasmodium: sporozoites (mosquito) → liver → merozoites → RBC → gametocytes → mosquito
HIV: CD4 receptor → reverse transcriptase → proviral DNA integration → new virions → CD4 depletion

subject: Biology
text: Explain the significance of double fertilisation in angiosperms.
modelAnswer:
Double fertilisation is unique to angiosperms. One sperm nucleus fuses with the egg cell to form the diploid zygote (2n) which develops into the embryo. The second sperm nucleus fuses with the diploid secondary nucleus (2n) to form the triploid (3n) primary endosperm nucleus, which develops into the nutritive endosperm.
Significance: Ensures that endosperm (food reserve) is produced only after fertilisation, preventing wastage of nutritive tissue if fertilisation does not occur.
keyPoints: Syngamy: sperm + egg = zygote (2n)
Triple fusion: sperm + secondary nucleus = PEN (3n)
Endosperm provides nutrition to developing embryo
Uniquely angiosperm feature

subject: Biology
text: Describe the process of spermatogenesis with the help of a neat labelled diagram.
modelAnswer:
Spermatogenesis occurs in the seminiferous tubules of the testes:
1. Spermatogonia (2n) multiply by mitosis and some differentiate into primary spermatocytes (2n).
2. Primary spermatocytes undergo meiosis I to form two secondary spermatocytes (n).
3. Secondary spermatocytes undergo meiosis II to form four spermatids (n).
4. Spermatids undergo spermiogenesis (differentiation) to form spermatozoa (sperms).
5. The sperms are released into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule (spermiation).
Diagram should show spermatogonium → primary spermatocyte → secondary spermatocyte → spermatid → spermatozoa.
keyPoints: Spermatogonia → primary spermatocyte (mitosis)
Primary → secondary spermatocytes (meiosis I)
Secondary spermatocytes → spermatids (meiosis II)
Spermatids → spermatozoa (spermiogenesis)

subject: Biology
text: What are the advantages of amniocentesis? State one ethical concern associated with it.
modelAnswer:
Amniocentesis is a prenatal diagnostic technique where amniotic fluid is withdrawn and foetal cells are analysed.
Advantages: (i) Detects chromosomal abnormalities like Down's syndrome (trisomy 21), Edwards' syndrome. (ii) Diagnoses metabolic disorders and genetic diseases in the foetus. (iii) Determines sex of the foetus.
Ethical concern: Amniocentesis is misused for sex determination and female foeticide, which is illegal in India under the PNDT Act (Prenatal Diagnostic Techniques Act).
keyPoints: Detects chromosomal abnormalities
Diagnoses genetic/metabolic disorders
Ethical concern: sex-selective abortion/foeticide
Banned for sex determination in India

subject: Biology
text: In a cross between parents having genotypes AaBb × AaBb, what fraction of the offspring will have (i) AABB genotype, (ii) AaBb genotype? State the law of independent assortment.
modelAnswer:
AaBb × AaBb:
For each gene independently: Aa × Aa gives 1/4 AA, 2/4 Aa, 1/4 aa.
(i) P(AABB) = P(AA) × P(BB) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.
(ii) P(AaBb) = P(Aa) × P(Bb) = 2/4 × 2/4 = 4/16 = 1/4.
Law of Independent Assortment: When two pairs of contrasting traits are combined in a hybrid, the factors of each pair segregate independently of each other during gamete formation, and different traits are inherited independently of each other.
keyPoints: AABB = 1/16 probability
AaBb = 4/16 = 1/4 probability
Apply independent assortment for each gene pair
State Mendel's Second Law

subject: Biology
text: Describe the lac operon model with a neat diagram, explaining what happens in the presence and absence of lactose.
modelAnswer:
Lac operon (Jacob and Monod) consists of: Promoter (P), Operator (O), and structural genes lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease), lacA (transacetylase).
Absence of lactose (repressed): The repressor protein (encoded by lacI) binds to the operator, blocking transcription. No mRNA is produced, no enzymes synthesised.
Presence of lactose (induced): Allolactose (inducer, derived from lactose) binds to the repressor. The repressor-inducer complex cannot bind to the operator. RNA polymerase transcribes the structural genes. β-galactosidase, permease, and transacetylase are produced to metabolise lactose.
This is an example of negative regulation (repressor system).
keyPoints: Components: promoter, operator, structural genes
Repressor binds operator in absence of lactose
Allolactose (inducer) inactivates repressor
Structural genes transcribed only when needed

subject: Biology
text: Explain Hardy-Weinberg principle and list any three factors that can cause deviation from this equilibrium.
modelAnswer:
Hardy-Weinberg principle states that allele and genotype frequencies in a population remain constant (at equilibrium) from generation to generation in the absence of disturbing factors.
If p = frequency of allele A and q = frequency of allele a (p+q=1), then genotype frequencies are: AA = p², Aa = 2pq, aa = q² (p²+2pq+q²=1).
Factors causing deviation (microevolution):
1. Genetic drift: random changes in allele frequency, especially in small populations.
2. Gene flow: immigration/emigration changes allele frequencies.
3. Mutation: creates new alleles.
4. Natural selection: differential reproductive success.
5. Non-random mating: changes genotype frequencies.
keyPoints: Allele frequencies constant across generations under ideal conditions
p²+2pq+q²=1 equation
Genetic drift, gene flow, mutation, natural selection, non-random mating disturb equilibrium

subject: Biology
text: Describe the life cycle of Plasmodium in the human host.
modelAnswer:
Plasmodium life cycle in humans:
1. Sporozoites are injected into blood by female Anopheles mosquito bite.
2. Sporozoites enter liver cells (hepatocytes) and undergo asexual reproduction (schizogony) → liver schizonts → merozoites (exo-erythrocytic stage).
3. Merozoites enter RBCs and undergo schizogony → ring stage → trophozoite → schizont → merozoites (erythrocytic stage).
4. RBCs rupture, releasing merozoites → fever, chills.
5. Some merozoites differentiate into gametocytes (sexual forms).
6. Gametocytes are ingested by mosquito to continue the cycle.
P. vivax causes relapse due to dormant hypnozoites in liver.
keyPoints: Sporozoite injection by Anopheles mosquito
Liver stage: exo-erythrocytic schizogony
Blood stage: erythrocytic schizogony causes fever
Gametocyte formation for sexual reproduction in mosquito

chapter: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
subject: Biology
text: What is somatic hybridisation? Give one example of a somatic hybrid.
modelAnswer:
Somatic hybridisation is the fusion of protoplasts (cells from which cell walls have been removed) of two different plant species to produce a hybrid cell, which can be grown into a new plant (somatic hybrid).
The process: Remove cell walls using cellulase and pectinase enzymes to get protoplasts. Fuse using PEG (polyethylene glycol) or electric stimulation. Culture the hybrid cell on medium.
Example: Pomato (potato + tomato) — somatic hybrid of Solanum tuberosum (potato) and Lycopersicon esculentum (tomato).
keyPoints: Protoplast fusion between different species
Cell wall removal by cellulase/pectinase
Fusion by PEG or electrofusion
Example: Pomato (potato + tomato)

subject: Biology
text: How do microbes help in sewage treatment? Describe the primary and secondary treatment.
modelAnswer:
Sewage treatment uses microbes to break down organic matter:
Primary treatment (physical): Sewage is passed through screens to remove large particles. Then through grit chambers. Finally, sedimentation in settling tanks produces primary sludge (heavy) and effluent.
Secondary treatment (biological): The effluent from primary treatment is aerated in aeration tanks. Aerobic bacteria form flocs and decompose organic matter into CO₂, H₂O. BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) is reduced by 90%. The activated sludge settles in secondary settling tanks.
The remaining water is passed through sand beds, chlorinated, and released or reused.
Sludge is anaerobically digested by anaerobes → biogas (CH₄+CO₂) + manure.
keyPoints: Primary: physical removal of solids
Secondary: aerobic bacteria reduce BOD
Floc formation by aerobic microbes
Anaerobic digestion of sludge → biogas

subject: Biology
text: Explain the role of the Ti plasmid in plant genetic engineering. What modification is made before using it as a vector?
modelAnswer:
Ti (tumour-inducing) plasmid from Agrobacterium tumefaciens is a naturally occurring vector for plant transformation. It carries T-DNA (transfer DNA) that integrates into the plant genome.
Normal Ti plasmid: Causes crown gall disease (tumour) due to T-DNA carrying genes for auxin/cytokinin synthesis.
Modification for use as vector:
1. The tumour-causing (oncogenic) genes in T-DNA are removed/disarmed to prevent tumour formation — creating a 'disarmed' Ti plasmid.
2. The desired foreign gene is inserted into the T-DNA region.
3. The recombinant Ti plasmid is introduced into Agrobacterium, which then infects plant cells.
4. T-DNA integrates into plant chromosomes, carrying the foreign gene.
keyPoints: Ti plasmid from Agrobacterium tumefaciens
T-DNA integrates into plant genome
Oncogenic genes removed to disarm the vector
Foreign gene inserted into T-DNA for plant transformation

subject: Biology
text: What are biodiversity hotspots? Name any two hotspots in India and give the criteria for declaring a region as a hotspot.
modelAnswer:
Biodiversity hotspots are regions with exceptional concentrations of endemic species that are also under significant threat of destruction.
Criteria (Norman Myers): A region must have at least 1500 species of endemic vascular plants AND must have lost at least 70% of its original habitat.
Two hotspots in India:
1. Western Ghats and Sri Lanka: High endemism in amphibians, reptiles, plants; major threat from deforestation.
2. Indo-Burma (Eastern Himalayas/NE India): Rich in mammals, birds, reptiles, plants.
(Also: Himalaya hotspot is sometimes listed separately.)
keyPoints: ≥1500 endemic vascular plant species + ≥70% habitat lost
Western Ghats and Sri Lanka hotspot
Indo-Burma hotspot (NE India)
Conservation priority regions

subject: Biology
text: What is ecological succession? Distinguish between primary and secondary succession with examples.
modelAnswer:
Ecological succession is the gradual and sequential change in the species composition of a community over time at a given area, until a stable climax community is established.
Primary succession: Occurs in an area where no life previously existed (bare rock, newly formed volcanic island). Very slow process; pioneer species like lichens initiate it.
Example: Succession on bare rock: lichens → mosses → grasses → shrubs → climax forest.
Secondary succession: Occurs in an area where organisms previously existed but were destroyed by a disturbance (forest fire, flood, ploughing).
Example: After a forest fire: grasses → shrubs → trees → climax forest. Faster than primary succession as soil already present.
keyPoints: Definition: sequential change in species composition
Primary: bare/lifeless area, slow, starts with lichens
Secondary: disturbed area with soil, faster
Both end with climax community

subject: Biology
text: What is eutrophication? How does it affect aquatic ecosystems?
modelAnswer:
Eutrophication is the process of enrichment of water bodies with nutrients (mainly nitrates and phosphates), leading to excessive growth of algae and aquatic plants.
Causes: Run-off of agricultural fertilisers, sewage discharge.
Effects: Algal blooms block sunlight, reducing photosynthesis for submerged plants. Decomposition of dead algae depletes dissolved oxygen (hypoxia/anoxia). This causes death of fish and other aquatic organisms. Biodiversity decreases. Water becomes turbid and foul-smelling. Cultural eutrophication (human-induced) accelerates the natural process.
keyPoints: Nutrient enrichment of water bodies
Algal bloom blocks sunlight
Decomposition depletes dissolved oxygen
Fish death and reduced biodiversity

subject: Biology
text: Name any two Cu-ion releasing IUDs. Explain any two ways by which these devices act as contraceptives.
modelAnswer:
Two Cu-ion releasing IUDs: (1) CuT (Copper T) (2) Cu7 (Copper 7) / Multiload 375

Two ways they act as contraceptives:
(i) Cu²⁺ ions released are toxic to sperms — they reduce sperm motility and suppress their fertilising capacity, preventing fertilisation.
(ii) They make the uterine environment unfavourable for implantation by causing changes in the uterine wall (endometrium), preventing implantation of the blastocyst even if fertilisation occurs.
keyPoints: CuT and Cu7/Multiload 375 are Cu-ion IUDs
Mechanism 1: Cu ions are toxic/spermicidal — reduce sperm motility; Mechanism 2: make uterine environment hostile to implantation

subject: Biology
text: A population of 200 fruit flies is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. The frequency of allele (a) is 0.4. Calculate: (i) Frequency of allele (A), (ii) Number of homozygous dominant fruit flies, (iii) Number of homozygous recessive fruit flies, (iv) Number of carrier fruit flies.
modelAnswer:
Given: q = 0.4 (frequency of a), total population N = 200

(i) Frequency of A: p = 1 − q = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6

(ii) Homozygous dominant (AA): p² × N = (0.6)² × 200 = 0.36 × 200 = 72 flies

(iii) Homozygous recessive (aa): q² × N = (0.4)² × 200 = 0.16 × 200 = 32 flies

(iv) Carrier (Aa) (heterozygous): 2pq × N = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 × 200 = 0.48 × 200 = 96 flies
keyPoints: p = 0.6; AA = 72; aa = 32; Aa (carriers) = 96
Hardy-Weinberg: p + q = 1; genotype frequencies p², 2pq, q²

subject: Biology
text: Jacob is genetically a carrier of the disorder that affects the shape of the RBCs (sickle-shaped cells). His son James suffers from the same disorder. (i) Give the biochemical reason for the disorder that changes the shape of the RBCs. (ii) Draw a Punnett square to show the genotype of the mother of James. (iii) Name and define the type of 'point mutation' responsible for this disorder.
modelAnswer:
(i) Sickle-cell anaemia: Glutamic acid (6th position in β-globin chain) is substituted by Valine due to a single nucleotide change. The mutant haemoglobin (HbS) polymerises under low-oxygen conditions, causing RBCs to become sickle-shaped.

(ii) Jacob (carrier) = HbA HbS; Mother of James must also be a carrier (HbA HbS) since James (HbS HbS) inherited HbS from both parents:
Punnett square:
       HbA    HbS
HbA: HbAHbA  HbAHbS
HbS: HbAHbS  HbSHbS
James (HbS HbS) can only arise if mother is also HbA HbS (carrier).

(iii) Type of point mutation: Missense mutation — a single nucleotide substitution (GAG → GUG / CTC → CAC at DNA level) that changes the codon so that a different amino acid (valine instead of glutamic acid) is incorporated into the protein.
keyPoints: Glutamic acid → Valine substitution in β-globin; HbS polymerises in low O₂ causing sickle shape
Mother must be carrier (HbA HbS); Missense mutation (single base substitution changes amino acid)

subject: Biology
text: The diagram shows three types of endosperms in angiosperms (Type 1: free nuclei/Nuclear, Type 2: Cellular, Type 3: Helobial). (a) Identify the three types of endosperms. (b) Name the type of endosperm which commonly occurs in polypetalous dicots.
modelAnswer:
(a) Three types of endosperms in angiosperms:
• Type 1 (Free nuclei) → Nuclear endosperm: divisions occur without cell wall formation initially, free nuclei in cytoplasm (e.g., coconut liquid endosperm)
• Type 2 → Cellular endosperm: cell wall formation occurs after each nuclear division (e.g., Datura, Adoxa)
• Type 3 → Helobial endosperm: first division produces a large micropylar cell and small chalazal cell; subsequent development differs; common in monocots (Helobiales)

(b) The type of endosperm common in polypetalous dicots is the Nuclear type (free nuclear endosperm).
keyPoints: Three types: Nuclear (free nuclei), Cellular, Helobial
Polypetalous dicots: Nuclear endosperm

subject: Biology
text: A male plant bearing red flowers was crossed with a female plant bearing yellow flowers. In the F₁ generation, all the flowers were orange in colour. (i) Give a reason to explain the change of colours in F₁ generation. (ii) Mention the ratio of red flowers, yellow flowers and orange flowers in the F₂ generation.
modelAnswer:
(i) The F₁ flowers are orange because of incomplete dominance. Neither the red (RR) allele nor the yellow (rr) allele is completely dominant over the other. In the heterozygous F₁ (Rr), both alleles are partially expressed, producing an intermediate orange phenotype.

(ii) F₂ generation (Rr × Rr):
• RR : Rr : rr = 1 : 2 : 1
• Phenotype: 1 Red : 2 Orange : 1 Yellow
• Ratio of red : yellow : orange = 1 : 1 : 2
keyPoints: Incomplete dominance — neither allele fully dominant; Rr gives intermediate orange
F₂ ratio: 1 Red (RR) : 2 Orange (Rr) : 1 Yellow (rr)
